title: Against All Oddities: Carry-On Coilovers from Japan?

body_markdown:
Every time I go to Japan for work, I try to be generous and bring home souvenirs. Usually the haul includes some weird ocean-critter-flavored snacks for my work colleagues, cookies for my wife, and car books I can’t interpret for my 2-year-old son. But #1 on my shop-for list is… my AE82 generation Corolla restoration project. My long-term plan is to recreate the car I[built and raced in high school](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/the-track-prepped-corolla-i-never-should-have-crushed/) and crushed in college.


Before I get to my most recent Japan trip, I need to tell you about my Corolla’s suspension. My previous recipe (back in the day) for better handling, if you could call it that, was a nightmare:


1. Obtain FX-16 GT-S strut assemblies
2. Cut apart and remove guts
3. Cut off spring perch and install Ground Control coilover sleeves
4. Obtain second generation MR2 or Porsche 911 Koni inserts (now $$$) and bolt in place from underside
5. Obtain camber plates from Lancer Evo and machine spacers
6. Modify strut towers to clear


Whew. I don’t want to go through all that again, and certainly not on all four corners. Why not coilovers? They seemed like a simpler route to the handling and stance that I wanted.


I checked the U.S. market for certain Chinese brands that offer coilovers for a huge roster of cars, but even those outfits didn’t have anything on hand that seemed easy. Not to mention the questionable quality. With the help of a friend, I located a set of brand-new coilovers from a company called Largus, that ships only within Japan. During the ordering process, I realized I was essentially getting a special, built-to-order piece. I guess it’s not every day that someone wants to slam a first-gen front-wheel-drive Corolla sedan on its guts.


My stalled AE82 project.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The coilovers arrived at my friend’s house in Japan after a few days. They lingered in his closet for some time before being transferred to another wardrobe, this one belonging to a guy who could attempt to bring the set to the U.S. via airplane as part of a future trip.


This plan did not go well. Upon scanning his baggage at the airport in Japan, officials informed him that transporting pressurized gas vessels in his checked baggage would be subject to hazardous materials regulation UN3164, Class 2.2 for compressed gas cylinders. The fine for getting caught by U.S. customs would have been roughly the cost of a starter home in America. With time ticking before his flight, he ran (literally) to FedEx and shipped them back to his apartment instead of throwing them in the bin with the discarded water bottles. A true friend. Back in the closet they went.


Loyal *Against All Oddities* readers may remember an earlier[Japanese souvenir adventure,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-a-souvenir-transmission-straight-from-japan/) in which I received a C160 six-speed Toyota gearbox and tore it down in a vintage Lambo shop in Yokohama. I then threw my back out while hauling the transmission on three trains, before bringing it home from Japan in two pieces of luggage.


Why not do something similar again?


On the plane flight to Japan for a recent work trip, I dug deep and found a potential loophole to the compressed gas cylinder regulation: the International Air Transport Association’s Provision A114. This section targeted the transport of shock absorbers specifically, permitting carry as long as the parts conform to certain pressure limits, gas volume, and won’t blow up like a pressure cooker bomb or fire off like a rocket due to poor quality.


After corresponding with Largus in a flurry of translated emails to verify and document all this, the company very politely told me to pound sand. Instead, I lovingly crafted a document detailing my assumptions on fill pressure, volume, and general explodability. I resolved to get to the airport very early to present the document (gently with both hands, per custom) to make my case and sort it out. The virtual chat personnel (or maybe bots) at JAL and American Airlines pointed to each other’s bag policies, which did not guarantee compatibility with Provision A114. My confidence was slowly eroding.


In the interim, I decided to maximize my free time in Japan with visits to museums. There, I was bludgeoned with AE82-related materials and exhibits: a NUMMI-assembled Nova at the Toyota Automotive Museum. Books and catalogs and sales brochures at the library. The universe was trying to tell me something. *Finish your car.*


An AE82 Chevy Nova assembled at the NUMMI plant in Fremont, California.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I hatched a new idea, which was more complicated in a sense but, in another sense, much simpler. Considering that the cost of shipping *just the coilovers* was roughly equivalent to shipping a complete car roll-on-roll-off… why not just buy and ship a whole car with a suitable suspension? Rather than going through all this trouble to build my standard AE82 sedan into a twin-cam GT spec car AND ship coilovers separately, why not just do it all at once?


Step 1 – Locate an AE82 GT sedan. Purchase it.
Step 2 – Extend trip by three days.
Step 3 – Install coilovers at that same Lambo shop.
Step 4 – Ship entire car.


After persistent online searching yielded nothing, my friend Hiro took me to a dealership for Showa-era cars in Yokohama, which seemed like the best shot at talking to people who might have the inside track in locating an AE82 GT Corolla. My head was absolutely spinning as I browsed what was essentially the parking lot of my wildest fantasies. Needing to seem somewhat serious (and not like a lunatic wandering the car park), I asked Hiro if he could approach the proprietors about a GT. And, while he was at it, assure them that I was a regular, cool guy.


Through Hiro’s interpretive skills, I learned that no one had seen a GT in years. Most had already been pulled apart for their valuable 4A-GE twin-cam engines and sold off for scrap. Honestly, that was probably for the best.


Not a Nova or Tempest… a Nissan Gloria Super.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The trip continued with a stop off at Uchiwa-san’s shop, where we had previously visited to tear down that C160 manual transmission. He had since moved on to other projects, which seemed even more challenging than smuggling shocks onto a commercial airplane. Namely, he was resurrecting of a Mitsubishi World War II tank engine that we spent about two hours poring over. On top of that was his rebuild of an all-aluminum Mazda 10A rotary engine, an Abarth 750 Zagato, and a Toyota 2000GT powerplant. All projects I would never trust myself with.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


We continued onto the infamous Daikoku parking area, which has been growing in notoriety as foreign tourists flock in to enjoy the car scene in Yokohama. They usually do so respectfully, but sometimes not. While dodging the influencers and rental R34 sedans with *Fast and Furious* paint jobs, I landed on some classic Daikoku rides: a pair of rear-wheel-drive AE86-platform Toyotas. One of them was the exact same color code as my four-door sedan at home and sported U.S.-spec diving board 5-mph bumpers along with Corolla badging. *Man, just like home!*


I ultimately decided to skip the risk of transporting the Largus coilovers in my luggage. In a rare moment of defeat, I allowed myself to shell out a four-figure sum for proper hazardous goods shipping. The only thing I took home with me was motivation to take this project across the finish line!
